name: PRF / PRP face contouring
lead: PRF and PRP face contouring refers to using platelet-rich plasma (PRP) or platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), concentrates made from a person's own blood, to improve the look of facial skin and, in some practices, to add subtle volume. In looksmaxxing and aesthetic circles the most common targets are dark under-eye circles, eye bags, fine lines, skin texture and a tired or hollow look, and the products are usually injected or applied after microneedling.

Platelet-rich plasma is a blood fraction with platelet levels typically 3 to 5 times normal, believed to release growth factors that aid healing [1]. Aesthetic clinics use it for wrinkles and fine lines, often with microneedling in the procedure popularised as the "vampire facial" [1]. PRF is a related product that also contains fibrin and, in its liquid injectable form (i-PRF), was introduced around 2014 [8]. Wikipedia describes the evidence for PRP overall as mixed [1].

People use these treatments for the look of the face by the chain: concentrated growth factors in the skin, stimulating repair and collagen, producing firmer, brighter or less hollow skin. Registered trials of platelet-rich fibrin mostly focus on dental and nerve applications; a small trial of PRF in a face cream is the nearest to cosmetic use [2].

paras: PRP is made by drawing blood and spinning it in a centrifuge to remove red cells while keeping platelets. Preparation varies between clinics and commercial kits, so the product differs by location [1]. PRP is typically grouped by leukocyte and fibrin content into leukocyte-rich PRP, leukocyte-reduced PRP and leukocyte-and-platelet-rich fibrin, which is the basis of PRF classification schemes [1][9].

PRF is prepared without anticoagulant, so it forms a fibrin matrix. Its solid clot form was the only version until 2014, when changes to centrifugation protocols and tube technology produced liquid injectable PRF (i-PRF) that can be injected like PRP [8]. A 2016 comparative study measured growth-factor release from PRP, PRF and advanced PRF [10].

Aesthetic medicine markets PRP for wrinkles, fine lines, blemishes and hair loss, based on claims about skin rejuvenation [1]. In the vampire facial, PRP is combined with microneedling, a format that spread in the 2010s with celebrity and media attention [1].

On looksmax.org, users discuss PRF for dark under-eye colour and eyebags. One thread titled as a PRF result presents it as the best treatment for those concerns and relays a doctor's preference for PRF over PRP [5]. Another user planned a PRF filler session for dark circles and promised to post updates, and a reply from a user who had tried it reported no change, suggesting it might help only if dark circles are age related [6]. A third thread describes a user making a personalised serum by adding PRP or PRF to a base cream after a vampire facial, noting the commercial version of the idea is expensive [7].

The vampire facial drew wide public attention in 2013 when Kim Kardashian West posted an Instagram photo of her blood-covered face during the procedure, which combines microneedling with topical PRP from the person's own blood; proponents say it stimulates skin cell growth and collagen, and she later said she regretted posting it.[16] Wikipedia states that the benefits claimed for vampire facials lack support from clinical studies, and describes the related literature on blood-based therapies as showing that autohemotherapy was used widely by dermatologists in the early 1900s before being dropped, with interest returning in the 2000s.[16]

Wikipedia's overview of PRP describes the evidence across medical uses as mixed, with tentative support in some conditions such as knee osteoarthritis and mixed results in tendon problems [1]. For aesthetic use it reports that PRP is marketed for wrinkles and skin rejuvenation but does not cite controlled results for facial contouring [1]. No registered trial tests PRF or PRP as a facial volume or contouring treatment [2][3][4][15][11].

Adverse effects are low in most trials [1]. In April 2024 the US CDC reported three women diagnosed with HIV after receiving facials at an unlicensed Albuquerque spa; about 200 other clients and partners tested negative, and investigators found the operator reused blood-contaminated single-use equipment without sterilisation, an infection-control failure [1].

Common effects described after these procedures are redness, swelling, bruising, tenderness, numbness and lumpiness at injection sites, which usually settle within about two days but can take a week or more with scabbing.[16] The main safety concern is treatment in non-medical settings by people untrained in infection control: in 2018 the New Mexico Department of Health warned that at least one business offering vampire facials could spread HIV, hepatitis B and hepatitis C, and the CDC later confirmed HIV transmission linked to such facials.[16]

In the United States the FDA does not regulate PRP itself, which is exempt from traditional pathways, so its clinical use is considered off label; the devices used to prepare it require clearance [1]. PRP gained media attention when athletes used it, and in 2011 the World Anti-Doping Agency removed intramuscular PRP from its prohibited list, citing lack of evidence of performance enhancement [1]. Branded vampire facials and PRP serums are sold in clinics and online, at prices that forum users describe as high [7].

The term platelet-rich plasma was first used in 1954. PRP blood banks appeared in the 1960s, and the material was used in transfusion medicine in the 1970s, in maxillofacial surgery about a decade later, and in Italian open-heart surgery in 1987 [1]. Interest in PRP for hair loss began around 2006 [1]. Injectable PRF followed in 2014 [8].

Registered studies include PRF in a face care cream for skin ageing (phase 2, n=20) [2], PRF in third molar surgery for swelling (n=31) [3], PRF with nerve repair after facial nerve injury (n=21) [4] and injectable PRF for gum thickness (n=13) and vestibular socket therapy (n=24) [15][11]. None of them tests PRF or PRP as a facial volume or contouring treatment.

Dental literature provides larger bodies of evidence for PRF. A 2017 systematic review covered PRF in regenerative dentistry, including intrabony defects, furcation defects and extraction sockets [12]. A 2024 network meta-analysis of randomised trials examined PRF for periodontal intrabony defects [13]. A randomised split-mouth trial of injectable PRF compared it with triamcinolone in 12 patients with oral lichen planus [14]. These studies concern oral tissues rather than the face's skin.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, PRF is discussed as a treatment for dark circles and under-eye bags and as a skincare-booster, with mixed personal reports [5][6][7].

claims.claim: PRF is the best treatment for dark under-eye colour and bags
claims.believers: A thread poster says a doctor prefers PRF to PRP and shows results for the under-eyes [5].
claims.experts: No registered trial tests PRF for under-eye circles; PRP evidence for skin overall is described as mixed [1].

claims.claim: PRF filler does little unless dark circles are age related
claims.believers: A user who received PRF filler for dark circles reported no change and said the mechanism only makes sense for age-related cases [6].
claims.experts: No controlled study of PRF for dark circles was found.

claims.claim: Adding PRP or PRF to a serum extends the benefits of a vampire facial
claims.believers: A user describes mixing blood-derived product into a base serum applied after microneedling to increase absorption [7].
claims.experts: The only registered cosmetic-adjacent trial is PRF in a face cream for skin ageing (n=20) [2].

claims.claim: Unlicensed PRP facials carry infection risk
claims.believers: Some users advise getting treatments from licensed clinics.
claims.experts: The CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to an unlicensed spa that reused contaminated equipment [1].

card.summary: Blood-derived concentrates injected for facial skin and volume; used in aesthetic clinics, with no trials of true contouring.
card.note: Preparation varies by clinic; infection control matters.

quick.overview:
PRP and PRF are made by spinning a person's own blood to concentrate platelets and growth factors, then injecting or applying them to the face.

They are marketed for skin rejuvenation; evidence overall is described as mixed.
quick.mechanism: Platelets release growth factors thought to stimulate tissue repair [1].
quick.risks: Adverse effects are generally low, though improper equipment reuse caused a 2024 HIV cluster at an unlicensed spa [1].

chain: A blood draw is spun to concentrate platelets (and fibrin for PRF)
The concentrate is injected or applied to the face, often after microneedling
Growth factors are thought to stimulate repair, giving firmer, brighter skin or smoother under-eyes
angle.text: People use PRP and PRF to improve skin texture, fine lines and dark or hollow under-eye areas, using their own blood as the active material. Results reported on forums vary from visible improvement to none.
